source.title: Gradient-Weight Alignment as a Train-Time Proxy for Generalization in Classification Tasks
source.authors: Florian A. Hölzl; D. Rueckert; G. Kaissis

record.tranche_reason: The study trains on randomized CIFAR-10 labels and reports validation performance at chance, alongside training on natural CIFAR-10 labels. This is a conceptual test of whether memorization and generalization can coexist, using a different measure and setup from V1.
record.gate_note: Figure 11 reports the randomized-label comparison relevant to V1. Early-stopping, robustness, sample-alignment, and estimator results do not directly test the other mapped versions. Hyperparameters in Table 4 are setup details, not results.
record.test_reason: Appendix A.4 uses the original random-label training comparison and held-out accuracy measure. Its results bear on V1, although they do not establish near-perfect training fit or matched recipes.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Appendix A.4, but not the paper's overall conclusion. The authors conclude that GWA offers an efficient training-time proxy for generalization, competitive early stopping, and sample-level diagnostics. They acknowledge distributional failure cases; with training-set size fixed, the 10% validation baseline outperforms GWA.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a randomized-label training condition with natural-label training to examine GWA dynamics; it does not report the matched architecture and recipe details required by V1.
record.method_sensitivity: Label condition (natural versus randomized); GWA exhibits a different time pattern under randomized labels.

fits_no_version.finding: GWA tracks validation performance, supports early stopping, distinguishes sample alignment, and exhibits a rise followed by decay during random-label memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-weight alignment provides a train-time diagnostic of generalization and memorization dynamics; it does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or the effect of removing memorized examples.

record.problems: The randomized-label passage does not identify the model architecture or provide exact training or validation accuracy values. The natural-label result is qualitative, and the text does not establish matched architecture and training recipe for the two conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results mapped to the versions were reported as direct tests. Early-stopping and robustness results in Sections 4.1–4.4 concern GWA as a proxy or selection method, rather than the mapped claim versions.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label training accuracy and coexistence under a verified identical architecture and training recipe, including the absence of explicit regularization, are not established.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers under comparable tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Missing evidence for full V1 is an untested component, not a demonstrated limitation or challenge. Optimizer settings, embedding-size analyses, and GWA comparisons do not independently test V2–V8.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not give exact training accuracy or test accuracy numbers for the natural-label and randomized-label comparison, and does not establish that the compared runs use the same architecture and recipe.
